title: Observability: logs, metrics and traces
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Logs, metrics and traces, one correlation id per request (Logback MDC, ContextVar), Micrometer and prometheus_client instruments, label cardinality, OpenTelemetry propagation and sampling.
source: SLF4J/Logback manual; Micrometer docs; Prometheus docs (histograms, naming); OpenTelemetry docs; W3C Trace Context; Python contextvars docs

questions.prompt: Checkout p99 jumped from 300 ms to 4 s. You want to know which downstream call inside one slow request ate the time. Which signal answers that most directly?

options.text: A distributed trace showing the spans of that request
options.why: Right: spans give a timed tree of the calls made for one request.

options.text: A counter of total HTTP requests handled, broken down per route
options.why: A counter shows volume, not where time went inside one request.

options.text: A gauge of JVM heap used over time
options.why: Heap trends say nothing about which call was slow.
Start-up logs are written once and cannot explain a runtime slowdown.

questions.explanation: Metrics say that something is wrong, traces say where, and logs say why. Interviewers like that ordering.

questions.prompt: Match each Micrometer / Prometheus instrument to the thing it is meant to record.

right.text: A value that only goes up, such as completed orders
A value that rises and falls, such as items in a queue
The distribution of request durations in buckets
One timed operation inside a trace
A free-text event with a timestamp

questions.explanation: Counters feed rate(); gauges are sampled snapshots; histograms let you compute percentiles; spans belong to tracing, not metrics.

questions.prompt: A counter http_requests_total has labels method (4 values), status (5 values) and route (25 values). Assume every combination occurs. Prometheus scrapes 10 instances and attaches an instance label to each series. How many time series does this one metric create?
questions.explanation: 4 x 5 x 25 = 500 combinations per instance, times 10 instances = 5,000. Adding a user_id label with 1,000 values would multiply that to 5,000,000, which is why unbounded ids never belong in labels.

questions.prompt: Write the body of a Spring OncePerRequestFilter.doFilterInternal(req, res, chain) that takes the id from the X-Request-Id header (or generates a UUID), puts it in the SLF4J MDC under "requestId", echoes it in the response header, and always cleans the MDC afterwards.

checks.label: reads the X-Request-Id header or generates a UUID
puts the id into MDC with MDC.put
removes the MDC entry in a finally block

questions.explanation: Server threads are pooled, so an MDC entry that is not removed leaks into the next request handled by that thread. The Logback pattern then prints %X{requestId}. Other shapes (a servlet Filter, a HandlerInterceptor) are equally valid.

questions.prompt: In a FastAPI app, write a ContextVar named request_id and an HTTP middleware that sets it from the x-request-id header (or a new uuid4 string) for the duration of the request and resets it afterwards.

checks.label: sets it from the header or uuid4
resets or clears it in finally

questions.explanation: ContextVar values follow asyncio tasks, unlike threading.local, so every log call in the request can read request_id.get() from a logging.Filter. Using structlog.contextvars.bind_contextvars is an equally good answer.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Log lines written from tasks submitted to an ExecutorService lose the request id unless you copy the MDC into the task.
questions.reason: SLF4J MDC is backed by a ThreadLocal, so each pool thread has its own, initially empty, context.

whys.a: Right: the ThreadLocal is why the context does not travel to another thread.
whys.b: They are related as cause and effect, not just two facts.
whys.c: The assertion is true: the id really is lost.
whys.d: The reason is true, so this cannot be the answer.

questions.explanation: Capture MDC.getCopyOfContextMap() before submitting and restore it inside the task (or use a TaskDecorator or the OpenTelemetry context wrappers).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: A Prometheus histogram can be used to estimate a fleet-wide p99 across many instances.
questions.reason: A summary exposes quantiles that were precomputed inside each client process.

whys.a: The summary fact does not explain why histograms aggregate.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but histograms aggregate because bucket counts can simply be added, which is a different reason.
whys.c: The reason is true, so option c cannot be right.
whys.d: The assertion is true: histogram_quantile over summed buckets works.

questions.explanation: Bucket counters add across instances, then histogram_quantile estimates the percentile. Precomputed summary quantiles cannot be averaged into a correct fleet quantile.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: The W3C traceparent header lets a trace continue across services written in different languages.
questions.reason: The traceparent header is understood only by the OpenTelemetry Java agent and is ignored by the Python SDK.

whys.a: The reason is false, so it cannot explain anything.
whys.b: The reason is false, not merely unrelated.
whys.c: Right: the header is a W3C standard honoured by all OpenTelemetry SDKs.
whys.d: The assertion is the true statement here, not the false one.

questions.explanation: traceparent carries version, trace id, parent span id and flags. Any compliant SDK can read it, which is the whole point of a standard.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Logging complete request and response bodies at INFO is a safe default for debugging.
questions.reason: Logs are routinely shipped to shared platforms that many engineers and vendors can read.

whys.a: The assertion is false, so R cannot be an explanation of a true statement.
whys.c: The reason is true, so option c is wrong.
whys.d: Right: bodies carry passwords, tokens and personal data, and the reason is exactly why that is risky.

questions.explanation: Log identifiers and outcomes, redact secrets and personal data, and turn body logging on only briefly at DEBUG.

questions.text: A trace is a tree of {1}. The {2} header carries the trace id between services. The OpenTelemetry Java {3} is attached with -javaagent and instruments common libraries without code changes.
questions.explanation: Spans are the nodes of the tree. Baggage is a different header that carries user-defined key/values.

questions.prompt: Which of these are good logging practices for a production API? Select all that apply.

options.text: Emit structured JSON lines with a requestId field
options.why: Right: structured fields are searchable and join with traces.

options.text: Return the correlation id to the caller in a response header
options.why: Right: support can quote it and you can find the exact request.

options.text: Log the full Authorization header to help debugging
options.why: Tokens in logs become credentials for anyone who reads the logs.

options.text: Use log levels so noisy detail can be switched off
options.why: Right: levels keep cost down and allow targeted DEBUG.

options.text: Log inside tight loops at INFO for every item
options.why: This floods storage and hides the signal.

questions.explanation: Good logs are structured, correlated, level-aware and free of secrets.

questions.prompt: A tracer configured with 1% head sampling means 1% of requests produce log lines.

options.why: Sampling affects which traces are exported, not what the logger writes.
Right: logs are separate from trace export. Head sampling decides at the start whether to record a trace.

questions.explanation: Tail sampling (decide after the trace completes) lets you keep every error and slow trace, which head sampling at 1% would mostly drop.

questions.prompt: With prometheus_client, define a Counter http_requests_total with labels method and status and a Histogram http_request_seconds, then record one GET that returned 200 taking the time of handle().
questions.model:
REQS = Counter("http_requests_total", "Requests", ["method", "status"])
LAT = Histogram("http_request_seconds", "Latency")
REQS.labels("GET", "200").inc()
with LAT.time():
    handle()
questions.explanation: Labels must come from a small closed set. observe(seconds) is the explicit alternative to the timer context manager.

questions.prompt: A service handles 1,000 requests per second and writes 2 log lines of 500 bytes per request. How many decimal gigabytes of log are written per day (one decimal place; 1 GB = 10^9 bytes)?
questions.explanation: 1,000 x 2 x 500 = 1,000,000 bytes per second, times 86,400 seconds = 86.4 GB. Multiply by retention days and replicas to size the log store.

questions.prompt: You use Spring Boot and want Prometheus to scrape JVM and HTTP metrics. What is the standard setup?

options.why: Right: Micrometer is the facade and this registry renders the Prometheus text format.

options.text: Write your own servlet that prints counters by hand in text format
options.why: Possible but pointless; Micrometer already instruments the framework.

options.text: Ship JFR files to Prometheus every minute
options.why: Prometheus scrapes text metrics; JFR files are a profiling format.

options.text: Enable DEBUG logging and parse the log for numbers
options.why: Parsing logs for metrics is fragile and costly.

questions.explanation: Also remember management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=prometheus so that the endpoint is exposed.
